bull.argument: Walmart's filing shows a business compounding its scale. Net sales rose 4.7% to $706.4 billion in fiscal 2026, and operating income grew to $29.8 billion from $29.3 billion. Walmart U.S. comparable sales increased 4.3%, with eCommerce contributing approximately 4.3 points, showing the omnichannel model is driving growth rather than cannibalizing it. Gross profit rate also improved 8 basis points, driven by disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses globally. Consolidated net income rose to $22.3 billion, lifting return on assets to 8.2% from 7.9%. The risk factors acknowledge that eCommerce investments will weigh on near-term results, but management is explicitly prioritizing returns on capital and margin expansion through productivity. Bears will point to a dip in ROI to 15.1% and a lower operating margin, yet ROI remains above 15% on a $310.7 billion invested capital base, and the decline is attributed to heavy investment in property and equipment that management expects to pay back over time.

claims.claim: Walmart U.S. eCommerce growth is contributing directly to comparable sales growth.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales positively contributed approximately 4.3% and 2.9% to comparable sales for fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively.

claims.claim: Gross profit rate improved in fiscal 2026, driven by disciplined inventory management.
claims.quote: The increase in fiscal 2026 was primarily driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, due to disciplined inventory management, as well as growth in higher margin businesses globally.

claims.claim: Return on assets rose, supported by higher net income.
claims.quote: The increase in ROA was primarily due to an increase in net income as a result of net increases in the fair value of our equity and other investments combined with higher operating income

bear.argument: The bull case rests on growth, but the filing shows the economics of that growth are getting harder to sustain. Operating income margin fell from 4.4% to 4.2%, and operating income grew only about 1.6% ($29.3B to $29.8B) on 4.7% sales growth, so profit is not keeping pace with revenue. Operating expenses rose to 20.9% of sales from 20.7%, driven partly by a roughly $0.9 billion increase in self-insured general liability claims and a $0.7 billion PhonePe share-based compensation charge. ROI declined to 15.1% from 15.5% as invested capital rose to $310.7 billion, and management attributes this to heavier property and equipment purchases whose payback is uncertain. The risk factors also warn that eCommerce, AI and automation spending will weigh on results in the short term, that failure to realize these benefits may hurt performance over the longer term, and that rising AI-enabled product search could reduce in-store traffic. Return on assets improved mainly because of net gains on equity investments, not operations.

claims.claim: Operating income barely grew while sales rose faster, so margin compressed
claims.quote: Operating income as a percentage of net sales 4.2 % 4.4 %

claims.claim: Returns on capital declined as invested capital grew through heavy capital spending
claims.quote: The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital due to higher purchases of property and equipment.

claims.claim: Investments may fail to pay off and could weigh on results and cause impairments
claims.quote: failure to realize the benefits of these investments may adversely impact our financial performance over the longer term

bull.argument: The bear's arithmetic is right: operating income rose about 1.6% against 4.7% sales growth, and the operating margin slipped to 4.2%. But the filing ties much of that squeeze to discrete items. The $0.9 billion rise in self-insured liability claims and the $0.7 billion PhonePe share-based charge are specific costs, and management says ROI benefited from improved business performance even after absorbing the PhonePe charge. Membership income grew strongly globally, and gross profit rate rose on disciplined inventory management. I concede the ROA gain came mainly from investment fair-value gains, not operations, so I do not rely on it. ROI fell only 40 basis points to 15.1% while invested capital expanded with property purchases that management frames as return-building. The risk factors are real: eCommerce and AI spending will weigh on results in the short term. But the filing shows the offsets already visible in comparable sales and membership growth, and a 15% return on $310.7 billion of invested capital is not the profile of a business losing its economics.

claims.claim: Management says ROI benefited from improved business performance, offset by a non-cash PhonePe charge.
claims.quote: ROI benefited from increased operating income due to improved business performance, which was partially offset by the incremental non-cash share-based compensation charge at PhonePe

claims.claim: Operating margin decline was attributed partly to factors that include strong growth in membership income.
claims.quote: primarily due to the factors described above and strong growth in membership income globally.

claims.claim: Gross profit rate improved in fiscal 2026 on disciplined inventory management.
claims.quote: The increase in fiscal 2026 was primarily driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, due to disciplined inventory management, as well as growth in higher margin businesses globally.

bear.argument: The bull's offsets are weaker than they look. The filing's own language shows the squeeze is not confined to one-off items. The self-insured liability increase is described as influenced by "rising costs to resolve claims across retail and related industries," which is an industry trend, not a discrete event. The filing also lists several charges that offset the business improvement: the PhonePe share-based charge, "certain legal matters and other business restructuring charges." Management is describing a cost base that is absorbing repeated pressure, not a clean recovery. Operating margin still fell, from 4.4% to 4.2%, while sales grew 4.7%. ROI fell from 15.5% to 15.1% as invested capital rose to $310.7 billion. The bull treats that capital as return-building, but the filing does not show when it will pay back. The risk factors are explicit that the cost of eCommerce, technology, talent and automation investments "will adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term," with benefits uncertain over the longer term. A 15% ROI is still healthy, but it is moving down while spending rises. That is a trend a shareholder should weigh.

claims.claim: The liability cost increase reflects an industry-wide trend rather than a one-time item
claims.quote: rising costs to resolve claims across retail and related industries

claims.claim: Several charges offset the business improvement, not just the PhonePe charge
claims.quote: ROI benefited from increased operating income due to improved business performance, which was partially offset by the incremental non-cash share-based compensation charge at PhonePe as well as certain legal matters and other business restructuring charges

claims.claim: Management expects investment costs to hit near-term results, with long-term payoff uncertain
claims.quote: the cost of certain investments in eCommerce, technology, talent and automation, including any operating losses incurred for those initiatives, will adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's evidence is more on-point to the core question of whether economics are deteriorating: margin compression, falling ROI against rising invested capital, and explicit short-term cost warnings. The bull concedes the ROA point and the arithmetic, then leans on offsets and membership income without quantifying them, so its response to the bear's 'multiple charges, not one-offs' argument is less convincing. The bear's rebuttal that the cost pressure is recurring and industry-wide was directly responsive to the bull's one-off framing.
